strengths: Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorems 1-2 uniquely characterize stable feature-learning parameterizations for PC as identical to BP's, constraining the design space meaningfully
Systematic framework using five desiderata that clearly derives constraints on scaling exponents through careful asymptotic analysis
Comprehensive experimental validation across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, CNNs, transformers) and datasets supporting theoretical predictions
Honest and thorough limitations discussion acknowledging gaps between linear theory and nonlinear practice, computational costs, and open questions
Provides theoretical justification for heuristic parameterizations in prior work, explaining why µP is the only scalable choice
Well-organized presentation with detailed appendix enabling reproducibility; code is made publicly available
weaknesses: Theory limited to linear networks while experiments only provide empirical evidence for nonlinearity; substantial gap between theoretical assumptions (exact equilibration) and practice (finite inference steps)

Main result—PC converges to BP under scalable parameterizations—provides no advantage over BP, and acknowledged instability of the fast saddle-to-saddle regime eliminates the primary proposed PC benefit

Practical applicability severely limited: requires ~100k inference steps per training step (making PC as slow as BP) and only 100 training steps shown (far from convergence); no final performance comparisons
Nonlinear experiments show brittleness: transformers required removal of layer normalization for convergence; missing error bars and limited architectural scope

Theory-practice gap insufficiently addressed: no analysis of finite-step inference dynamics, unclear what 'activity equilibrium seems to be reached' means operationally, no convergence rate characterization
N ≫ L regime is restrictive and impractical for realistic architectures; paper doesn't clarify minimum width-to-depth ratios needed or applicability to standard models like ResNet-50

strengths: Rigorous mathematical analysis: Systematic derivation of stability desiderata for PC using established frameworks, with careful treatment of width and depth constraints
Comprehensive scope: Extends analysis from MLPs to residual networks and width-only to width+depth regimes, showing generality of parameterization constraints
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with good motivation and informative visualizations of main theoretical results
Empirical breadth: Validates theory across multiple architectures (ResNets, CNNs, Transformers) and datasets, showing approximate convergence for nonlinear networks
Honest limitations discussion: Authors explicitly state when theory applies (linear networks, equilibrated activities, N >> L) and acknowledge gaps
weaknesses: Severe scope limitation: All theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1-2) apply only to linear networks; nonlinear results are purely empirical without theoretical justification

Strong unjustified assumptions: Theory requires exact activity equilibrium (∂F/∂z*=0), which is unlikely in practice and not rigorously analyzed when violated; transformer experiments required removing layer normalization to maintain convergence
Restrictive N >> L condition: The requirement for width much larger than depth significantly limits applicability; Figure 1 shows convergence is still imperfect even at N=512, L=32

Negative practical implications: Under stable parameterizations, PC only recovers BP gradients (no advantage); 'Takeaway 2' proves the only prior regime where PC outperforms BP (fast saddle-to-saddle) is unstable with both width and depth

Insufficient experimental validation: All nonlinear experiments train for only 100 steps before convergence; no end-to-end training or downstream task evaluation; no demonstration of practical scalability benefits claimed in abstract

Incremental novelty: Primarily extends Ishikawa et al. (2024) by proving uniqueness of μP parameterization for PC and Innocenti et al. (2025) by theoretically justifying their α=1/2 approach; uses standard Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022b) analysis framework
Unresolved practical limitations: PC inference requires ~depth-many iterations; paper speculates analog hardware could help but provides no evidence; this critical bottleneck remains unaddressed

Misleading biological plausibility claims: Paper claims results show how brain implements BP locally, but theory is linear-only, requires equilibrium convergence, and hasn't verified N >> L in actual brains
Heuristic extensions to practice: CNN and transformer parameterizations (§A.6) are heuristics not derived from theory, creating gap between linear theory and modern architectures
Missing critical experiments: No analysis of inference cost scaling; no measurement of actual sample efficiency or wall-clock training time vs BP; no experiments on when/how theory breaks down

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis with systematic derivation of Theorems 1-2, carefully verifying all five desiderata for stability. Mathematically sound and non-trivial.
Novel result that PC and BP admit identical sets of width- and depth-stable parameterisations—this is more constraining and insightful than merely showing equivalence.
Comprehensive experimental validation across architectures (linear/nonlinear MLPs, ResNets, CNNs, transformers) and datasets (toy, CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, ImageNet), consistently supporting theory.
Well-motivated biological application: demonstrates BP can be implemented with local updates in wide networks (width ≫ depth), aligning with brain architecture.
Clear, well-organized presentation with accessible background. Honest discussion of limitations and gaps between theory and practice.
Practical impact through principled guidance on parameterisations, already influencing recent work (Innocenti et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Limited practical advantages demonstrated: main result is constraining (PC must copy BP parameterisations) rather than enabling. The unique PC advantage (saddle-to-saddle escape) is shown to be unstable.

Significant theory-practice gap: theory assumes linear networks or exact activity equilibrium; practice uses nonlinear networks with finite inference steps that don't reach equilibrium. Convergence degradation without perfect equilibrium is not quantified.

Computational cost of PC inference inadequately addressed: experiments report 100k inference iterations for deep models before each weight update. This remains prohibitively expensive; speculation about analog hardware doesn't justify current applicability.

Experiments train for only 100 steps (acknowledged limitation), preventing assessment of convergence on realistic tasks. ImageNet results show only brief training windows. Transformer experiments require removing layer normalisation, limiting relevance to practical models.
Heuristic extensions for CNNs, transformers, and Adam lack theoretical justification. While empirically validated, they're not principled derivations and may not generalise.
Limited scope: analysis restricted to specific 'abcd' parameterisation framework. Doesn't explore whether fundamentally different parameterisations could exist within broader frameworks.

Missing experimental analyses: no sensitivity studies, limited characterization of equilibrium convergence speed, informal discussion of why certain regimes are 'unstable', unclear what tolerance on approximate equilibrium preserves convergence guarantees.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis deriving stable PC parameterizations through systematic verification of five desiderata; first principled framework for PC scaling with depth
Stronger results than prior work (Ishikawa et al. 2024): proves μP is the unique stable and feature-learning parameterization, not just showing existence
Comprehensive experimental validation: systematic width/depth sweeps, multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, ImageNet), modern architectures (CNNs, transformers), proper random seed averaging
Novel extension to depth-aware parameterizations with joint N,L→∞ limits and O(L/N) convergence rates for gradients; clean connection to recent BP theory extensions
Well-organized presentation with clear main results and practical implications; thorough appendix with detailed proofs; code made available for reproducibility
Identifies important practical issue: standard PyTorch parameterizations cause PC outputs to explode with width, providing actionable guidance
weaknesses: Core theoretical results (Theorems 1-2) restricted to linear networks; nonlinear validation is empirical rather than theoretical, limiting guarantees for practical architectures

Critical assumption of exact PC inference convergence (∂F/∂z*=0) not fully justified: experiments use finite iterations, convergence rates not analyzed, and Innocenti et al. (2025) reported deterioration of energy-loss correspondence during training
Restrictive L/N→0 requirement for depth results: standard architectures (Transformers, ResNets) have comparable L and N; results only meaningful for unusually wide-and-shallow networks

Limited practical impact: no demonstration that PC can train to convergence on real tasks; all large-scale experiments train for only 100 steps; computational cost of inference underexplored and potentially prohibitive
Heuristic extensions to practical settings: CNN/transformer parameterizations adapted from other work without theoretical justification; Adam learning rate scaling stated but not derived
Biological plausibility claims overstated: brain has comparable width and depth (doesn't satisfy L/N→0), and attention mechanisms are non-local, both violating key assumptions

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorems 1-2 provide clean characterizations of stable and feature-learning parameterizations for PC, with detailed proofs. The mathematical framework is well-established and sound.
Addresses important gap: Provides theoretical justification for heuristic parameterizations in prior work (Innocenti et al. 2025, Ishikawa et al. 2024).
Comprehensive scope: Analysis covers MLPs, residual networks, and extends to practical architectures (CNNs, transformers) with experiments spanning toy tasks to large-scale benchmarks.
Honest treatment of limitations: Section 6.3 clearly acknowledges linearity assumption, inference cost, biological implausibility, and limitations of the saddle-escape regime (Takeaway 2).
Systematic presentation: The parameterization framework and three desiderata are well-motivated and clearly presented with appropriate visual aids.
weaknesses: Limited novelty—PC reduces to BP: Central finding shows stable PC parameterizations are identical to BP (Theorems 1-2) and PC gradients converge to BP gradients (Corollaries 3.2-4.2). This undermines PC motivation: if PC must equal BP at scale, why incur the inference overhead? The paper doesn't discover PC-specific phenomena but shows PC must become BP.

Theory-practice gap: All theoretical results are for linear networks only; nonlinear extensions are heuristic. Figure 4 only demonstrates gradient alignment, not convergence. Equilibrated energy is closed form only for linear networks; practical inference convergence not guaranteed.

No demonstrated practical advantages: PC only matches BP in the L/N→0 regime (extremely wide networks), where BP is algorithmically simpler. The only prior PC advantage (fast saddle escape) is shown to be unstable. Paper doesn't train to convergence on realistic tasks due to inference cost (~100k iterations for deep models, matching or exceeding model depth).

PC-specific objective vanishes: The rescaling factor s(θ) approaches 1 at scale (s(θ)=1+O(N^{-1}) for MLPs, s(θ)=1+O(L/N) for ResNets), making the PC energy indistinguishable from BP loss. Rather than discovering PC phenomena, theory shows PC loses distinguishing features.

Incomplete equilibrium analysis: Theory assumes exact convergence z* where ∂F/∂z*=0. In practice, inference uses finite iterations with no quantitative characterization of approximation error. Deep models require 100k inference iterations (practically impractical), and sensitivity to incomplete convergence not addressed.

Limited experimental scope: Only 100 training steps for nonlinear models; no convergence to good performance demonstrated; no wall-clock time comparisons to BP; hyperparameter transfer property not validated; only gradient alignment shown, not learning efficiency.

Oversold biological plausibility: Convergence requires L/N→0 (plausible architecturally) but inference cost appears biologically implausible (~100k iterations per sample). Speculation about analog hardware is unsubstantiated.

Alternative parameterizations under-explored: Constrains analysis to one parameterization family (Eqs. 7-10). Figure A.5 suggests other stable parameterizations exist but aren't investigated. Potential PC-specific parameterizations not explored.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving that stable feature-learning parameterizations for linear PCNs are identical to those for BP (Theorems 1-2), with uniqueness within the considered framework—a genuine advance beyond prior existence results

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (MLPs, ResNets, CNNs, transformers), datasets (toy, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, Tiny Shakespeare), optimizers, and loss functions consistently supporting theoretical predictions
Novel extension to joint width-depth limits with L/N→0 regime and principled α=1/2 scaling for residual networks, addressing practical deep network architectures
Clear practical implications: the paper demonstrates standard parameterizations fail for PC (like BP) and provides theoretically-grounded remedies applicable to practitioners
Thorough mathematical treatment with systematic verification of all desiderata; detailed proofs in appendix show methodical and convincing analysis
Strong biological motivation addressing how BP could be implemented with local learning rules in wide networks, with implications for neuroscience
Well-written main paper with good intuition alongside formal results; effective figures (1-3) clearly illustrate key findings
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis restricted to linear networks; while nonlinear experiments (Section 5) provide heuristic support, they lack theoretical guarantees, leaving significant theory-practice gap

Theory assumes exact activity equilibrium (∂F/∂z*=0), which is impractical; iterative optimization in experiments shows heuristic validity but lacks guarantees. Up to 100k inference iterations for deep models raises serious practical concerns

No clear evidence of PC advantages: paper shows PC→BP asymptotically but doesn't establish when to use PC. The potentially beneficial 'fast saddle-to-saddle' regime is shown to be unstable with width/depth (Takeaway 2). All experiments limited to 100 steps due to computational cost
Critical inference cost bottleneck remains unresolved; while analog hardware and acceleration strategies mentioned, these are speculative and leave uncertain path to practical efficiency
Convergence results apply only to L/N→0 regime (increasingly wide-than-deep). Modern LLMs have L/N ratios of 10-100×, not approaching limit. Approximation tightness for practical networks unclear
Heuristic extensions to CNNs and transformers (Section A.7) lack theoretical justification, limiting theoretical rigor in practically relevant settings
Parameterization analysis limited to 'abcd' framework with specific desiderata; other stable parameterizations might exist where PC doesn't converge to BP (acknowledged in Section 6.3)

Biological plausibility narrative undermined by: (1) transformer attention being inherently non-local, (2) removal of layer normalization breaking standard practices, (3) exact PC algorithm may not be biologically implementable
Linear theory uses gradient flow while experiments use discrete optimizers (GD, Adam); this theory-practice gap, though standard, is not addressed
